title: What Did People in Edo Japan Actually Do All Day?

shots.narration: You wake up in Edo with yesterday's work still waiting.
shots.action: Blue sits awake on the ONE original navy cushion at the LEFT side of the unchanged low table. Table is empty. Bedding stays fully stacked on the left recess, gray teapot beside it. No second cushion.

shots.narration: A wooden box needs its lid fitted.
shots.action: Use the unchanged approved empty location master as the establishing environment for this narration.

shots.narration: Your breakfast needs water.
shots.action: Blue stands next to the fixed well holding one empty wooden bucket, no extra people.

shots.narration: And the room where you slept is about to become somewhere to eat, sort belongings, and get ready to earn a living.
shots.action: Red stands behind the RIGHT half of the original table, putting the same folded gray garment onto its right half with both white oval mittens. Navy cushion stays under LEFT table half; bedding and teapot left unchanged. Table otherwise empty.

shots.narration: The lid catches at one corner.
shots.action: Blue sits behind the unchanged workbench testing the matching rimmed lid against the SAME wide shallow wooden box in the final prop reference. Copy the exact joints and proportions; no cube. Entire white head visible, two white oval mitten hands. Hand plane left, mallet and chisel right.

shots.narration: It is a small problem, but it belongs to someone expecting the finished box.
shots.action: Blue examines the slightly lifted SAME matching lid over that SAME wide shallow box at the original bench center. Keep all box joints/proportions, hand plane left, mallet/chisel right. Full head and unchanged neck towel.

shots.narration: Today, skill will show itself in a clean fit rather than a spectacular object.
shots.action: Blue holds the SAME rimmed matching lid just beside the SAME wide shallow box at bench center, examining its wooden joints. No cube, no second box, no added nails. Original tools remain in their places.

shots.narration: Before you can deal with it, the household has a morning to get through.
shots.action: Blue stands behind the LEFT half of the table holding the gray rolled tool wrap from the last input, with its one tie and wooden handle ends. Red stands behind the RIGHT half holding ONE EMPTY small woven shopping basket. Gray folded garment stays on table right from shot 004. Keep ONE navy cushion under the table left.

shots.narration: Meanwhile, someone in the household is deciding what to buy, what can wait, and whether a small repair will bring in anything useful. A city does not run on heroic poses. It runs on people remembering the things they still have to do.
shots.action: Red stands beside the vegetable stall, carrying a small empty woven basket, considering the produce without taking any.

shots.narration: We are in Edo, the city that would later become Tokyo, around the year seventeen hundred. The Tokugawa shogunate has its seat here. But the people making the streets busy are not all warriors. Artisans, merchants, servants, and laborers give the city its daily motion.
shots.action: Wide empty canonical wooden bridge and adjoining timber city, with a few distant anonymous adult white-headed townspeople walking; no cast foreground.

shots.narration: Come through one ordinary working day with an imagined artisan household. Their particular errands are our route through the city, not a schedule every resident followed. A rich merchant, a servant, and a poor worker could inhabit very different Edos, sometimes on the same street.
shots.action: Blue and Red stand outside their fixed alley doorway. Blue carries the EXACT gray rolled tool wrap with tie and wooden handle ends in the final prop reference; no blue bundle, gray handbag, shoulder bag or rectangular suitcase. Red carries the same small EMPTY woven shopping basket. No other people.

shots.narration: How much of this day can you call your own? Keep that question in mind while the household gets ready. Some hours will earn money. Others will keep everyone fed and supplied. Somewhere between them, there may be room for a cup, a conversation, or a look at the water.
shots.action: Blue and Red sit calmly with two plain tea cups at the canonical riverside bench; restful posture, no exaggerated smiles.

shots.narration: First, the bed has to disappear. Not into a separate bedroom, but out of the way. You fold the bedding and return it to its place. The same stretch of floor can now serve another purpose. Nothing about the room has changed. What you can do in it has.
shots.action: Blue crouches at the LEFT bedding recess and folds the existing navy top quilt onto that stack. Gray teapot remains beside bedding. ONE navy cushion stays under table LEFT; table empty, not moved.

shots.narration: Paper panels soften the light. Timber frames the walls. The low table is within reach of the bedding, and your belongings are close enough that you cannot forget them for long. The room is modest. Some rented homes were tighter still, while better-off households had very different surroundings.
shots.action: Use the unchanged approved empty location master as the establishing environment for this narration.

shots.narration: The Edo-Tokyo Museum describes many commoners living in divided row houses called nagaya. The important word is divided. Several households could occupy sections of one long building. You might have your own doorway, but your domestic life did not unfold far from other people's domestic lives.
shots.action: Canonical shared alley, identical timber walls and plain sliding doors, a few distant adult white-headed residents entering their own doors.

shots.narration: For this household, setting things down is already a small decision. A basket left in the wrong place occupies the route to the door. A bundle on the table competes with breakfast. In a room with several jobs, tidiness is not decoration. It is access.
shots.action: Red stands at table right and sets the ONE EMPTY woven basket on the floor just INSIDE the RIGHT doorway. The folded gray garment stays at table right. Original cushion left remains in place. No new cushion.

shots.narration: Outside, another door opens. Somebody carries a bucket past you. The museum emphasizes the different occupations and mutual assistance within these neighborhoods. That does not make every neighbor your best friend. It means the people around you are part of the practical world you have to navigate.
shots.action: Blue stands at the doorway while one anonymous adult white-headed resident in muted green long sleeves and trousers passes with a wooden bucket.

shots.narration: Before the meal comes the water. Take the bucket to the shared well. It will serve more than one task when it reaches the house, so leaving this errand until later means leaving something else waiting too. The route is short; the dependence on it is substantial.
shots.action: Blue stands at the fixed well in the alley, holding one empty wooden bucket by its simple handle.

shots.narration: Edo's water supply was more engineered than the romantic image of a premodern city might suggest. The Tokyo Waterworks Bureau describes water carried through stone and wooden conduits to waterworks wells, where residents drew it for drinking and household use. The bucket is the visible end of a larger system.
shots.action: Close framing on the fixed shared well with wooden rim, simple rope and bucket, adjacent timber wall unchanged; no transparent cutaway or new pipes.

shots.narration: That system did not fit inside one neighborhood. The Tamagawa waterworks, completed in the seventeenth century, brought water toward the city from far away. Behind the familiar household gesture of lifting a bucket stood channels, construction, maintenance, and the problem of supplying an expanding population.
shots.action: Use the unchanged approved empty location master as the establishing environment for this narration.

shots.narration: At the well, you lower the bucket and bring it up full. Set it down before adjusting your grip. Your partner arrives with another vessel and waits for space. Household errands have already become a small negotiation over a common facility.
shots.action: Blue sets a filled wooden bucket on the ground next to the fixed well, Red waits a pace away holding an empty smaller bucket; no spilling.

shots.narration: The water reaches the doorway. There is relief in setting the bucket down safely. A task that occupied your hands and attention is finished for now. The next question is what needs the water first, because food does not prepare itself just because its ingredients have arrived.
shots.action: Red stands in the fixed RIGHT home doorway, holding the wooden water bucket with both mitten hands. Empty woven basket already rests on floor inside that doorway. No meal on table yet, table otherwise cleared; original navy cushion left.

shots.narration: Breakfast is rice, soup, and vegetables at a cleared table. This household's meal gives us a starting point, not a fixed menu for every resident. Income and circumstances made a difference. What everyone sharing this table can agree on is that sitting down now feels better than carrying the water did.
shots.action: Blue and Red sit at the canonical low table with exactly two small plain bowls of rice, two plain soup bowls and one small dish of vegetables.

shots.narration: The Tokyo Metropolitan Library traces Edo's food culture to agriculture, fishing, and distribution networks linking the city with surrounding communities and more distant regions. A bowl placed in front of you therefore connects the home to people and places you will not meet this morning.
shots.action: Use the unchanged approved empty location master as the establishing environment for this narration.

shots.narration: You eat. For a moment, the tasks that produced the meal are out of sight. The water has been carried. The ingredients are here. The table has been cleared. That brief feeling of having everything in reach is pleasant partly because somebody has arranged it.
shots.action: Continue the EXACT breakfast state in the last approved meal image: Blue still kneels on original navy cushion LEFT, Red on bare tatami RIGHT, at the SAME original table. Red lifts her own rice bowl with one smooth mitten and chopsticks in the other; Blue remains quietly eating. Keep BOTH soup bowls, Blue's rice bowl, ONE central vegetable dish and the same chopsticks; Red's rice bowl is in her hand, not duplicated. NO fish, extra cups, new cushions or additional food.
shots.accepted_variant: Targeted continuity retry; original trial retained, not selected.

shots.narration: Before leaving, you check what remains for later. There is enough to plan around, but an extra purchase may help. Your partner takes the basket. The choice will depend on what a seller has available and what else the household needs its money to do.
shots.action: Continue that same breakfast with BOTH Blue and Red in their exact seats. Blue looks into ONE newly opened small wooden food container placed at table left beside his rice and soup bowls. Red holds the original empty woven shopping basket at her side, preparing to leave. Keep the two rice bowls/two soup bowls and ONE vegetable dish; no fish or second cushion.

shots.narration: You step out fed, equipped, and already involved in other people's mornings. Someone else's bucket is on its way home. A doorway is being swept. The street beyond will not wait until every household has finished breakfast. Daily life overlaps; it does not proceed one scene at a time.
shots.action: Blue walks out of his original alley doorway carrying the EXACT gray rolled tool wrap shown in the last input: one cloth tie and wooden handle ends. No navy wrap, purse, gray suitcase or shoulder bag. One distant covered white-headed adult sweeps at another doorway.

shots.narration: A bell sounds outside. The Edo-Tokyo Museum describes bells of time that gave residents an approximate hour. It is a public reference carried through the air, reaching people who are occupied with very different things. You hear it on your way to a piece of unfinished work.
shots.action: Blue pauses and turns his head, still holding the same gray rolled tool wrap from 027.

shots.narration: There is another difference. As the Seiko Museum explains, Edo-period Japan used a seasonal system: daylight and night were each divided into six parts. Those units changed length with the season. Time was organized, but it was not your modern sequence of equal sixty-minute appointments.
shots.action: Use the unchanged approved empty location master as the establishing environment for this narration.

shots.narration: Elsewhere, shops are open and sellers are moving. The Tokyo Metropolitan Library describes itinerant merchants carrying wares through Edo's streets, as well as food stalls. Commerce can come toward the customer. For a busy household, that matters almost as much as having a large shop nearby.
shots.action: Red watches the passing shoulder-pole vendor while still holding the SAME empty round handled woven basket from 009.

shots.narration: Walk a little farther and the city looks different. Routes connect doorways, shops, bridges, and landing places. The same person might be a neighbor at home, a supplier on the street, and a customer elsewhere. Ordinary people give those places their meaning by passing between them.
shots.action: Blue walks across the fixed wooden bridge carrying that EXACT gray rolled tool wrap with ONE tie and wooden handle ends. No gray suitcase, handbag or navy bag. Two distant covered white-headed adults walk the other way.

shots.narration: At the workbench, the troublesome corner is still troublesome. Bring the lid down carefully and feel where it catches. The correction must happen in the wood, not in an argument with the customer. You set the lid aside and prepare to work on the edge.
shots.action: Blue sits behind fixed bench testing that SAME matching rimmed lid on the SAME wide shallow joined box. It has the exact proportions of the final box reference, not a new cube. Original tools retained.

shots.narration: Tokyo's account of Edo sashimono describes furniture and smaller wooden objects assembled using carefully worked joints rather than nails. The craft developed across the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries. Not all woodworking was sashimono. But it gives us a useful way to see skill in a small, ordinary object.
shots.action: Close shot at fixed workshop bench: a simple small wooden box corner with clean interlocking wooden joints and matching plain lid, no metal nails, no people.

shots.narration: You check the edge, position the board, and take off a little material. A shaving lands on the bench. Then you stop and test the fit, because removing more is easy and putting it back is not. The useful rhythm is action, inspection, and another small adjustment.
shots.action: Blue uses the SAME wooden hand plane from original bench left on one newly placed thin plain board at bench left. The SAME wide shallow box and its matching lid remain at bench center/right, visible and unchanged. Original mallet and chisel remain right; only modest wood shavings.
shots.accepted_variant: Targeted continuity retry; original trial retained, not selected.

shots.narration: The parts that will disappear inside the finished box still matter. A customer may admire the outside, but a poor fit can reveal itself every time the object is used. This is one reason the official description emphasizes workmanship even in places that remain unseen.
shots.action: True object insert, derived from the approved box-design reference. Keep EXACTLY the SAME wide shallow box open, same corner joints and matching rimmed lid beside it on the SAME bench, hand plane left, mallet/chisel right. NO people and NO anatomy. No redesign of box; no new camera angle, just tighter crop on the objects.

shots.narration: You try the lid again. Better. The change is tiny enough that someone arriving now might not notice what occupied you. From outside, a worker can look as though he is merely sitting. From the bench, the whole morning has been a sequence of decisions.
shots.action: Blue places the matching lid flat onto the small box with both white mitten hands; calm focused posture, box fits without fantasy glow or motion effects.

shots.narration: Your partner arrives at the doorway carrying a folded garment. It needs a small repair before it goes back to its owner. You make space on the bench for a quick look. The household now has two pieces of work to complete, each demanding a different kind of care.
shots.action: Red stands in the existing right workshop doorway holding the SAME folded gray garment parcel. Blue is out of this shot. The SAME finished wide shallow joined box and its matching lid CLOSED remain at original bench center, hand plane left, mallet/chisel right.
shots.accepted_variant: Targeted continuity retry; original trial retained, not selected.

shots.narration: For a moment, the two jobs share a space. The box is almost ready. The cloth can be examined. A conversation about today's errands interrupts neither occupation very dramatically, yet it helps arrange what comes next. Work is not always sealed off from domestic life by a separate building.
shots.action: Blue sits behind the unchanged bench and Red stands next to its RIGHT side holding the SAME folded gray garment parcel. SAME completed wide shallow wooden box with matching lid CLOSED on the bench. Original hand plane, mallet and chisel remain. Two neutral faces, no dialogue text.

shots.narration: While that box leaves the bench, another piece of work is less conspicuous. A seam is being checked. A usable garment is laid out rather than discarded. For our household, the point is practical: can the thing do its job again without buying a replacement today?
shots.action: Red kneels on BARE tatami at RIGHT side of original table, inspecting the same unfolded gray garment laid on table right. ONE small plain wooden sewing box on table left. Original navy cushion remains EMPTY under table left; original bedding/gray teapot unchanged.

shots.narration: She folds the garment after checking it. Outside, clothing belongs to a much wider world than this modest repair: trade, changing taste, and the desire to be seen a certain way. The Tokyo Metropolitan Library treats the evolving culture of dress as a significant part of Edo life.
shots.action: Red remains kneeling on BARE tatami at RIGHT side of table, folding the same repaired gray garment on table right. Keep the same small wooden sewing box on table left. EMPTY original navy cushion stays under table left, no new cushions.

shots.narration: By the time she reaches the street, the repaired cloth is just one of several things to remember. Return the parcel. Buy something for the meal. Bring the basket home. An errand can look like a stroll from a distance, especially if you cannot see the list inside the person's head.
shots.action: Red passes fixed market stall carrying ONE woven shopping basket with the folded repaired GRAY garment parcel inside. Retain basket handle, size and plain gray cloth. No purchased greens yet.

shots.narration: A shopfront can offer temptation as well as necessity. A fine piece of cloth may catch your eye without coming anywhere near your budget. Looking is not the same as buying. Some of the city's pleasures can be borrowed for a moment simply by passing them.
shots.action: Red carries that SAME woven basket with folded GRAY garment parcel still inside, looking toward THREE muted folded fabrics on the existing interior shelf. Do not empty the basket or remove it. No purchases, no extra people.

shots.narration: The gap between having money and displaying it mattered, too. The Asian Art Museum describes attempts to restrain commoners' luxury, alongside their ways of negotiating those restrictions. Status was not a simple photograph of wealth. An expensive-looking life and an officially privileged life were not always the same.
shots.action: Red still holds that SAME basket with folded GRAY garment parcel inside near the existing textile shop doorway. Three muted folded fabrics on shelf. One distant adult white-headed merchant in covered plum clothing passes; no jewelry. Do not remove or empty Red's basket.

shots.narration: For this day, no grand purchase follows. The basket comes home with a few ingredients instead. That is not a defeat. It is the choice that lets the household move from one meal to the next. The city offers more possibilities than one ordinary day can afford.
shots.action: Returned-shopping illustrative crosscut: both partners at unchanged empty table; ingredient basket on floor inside right doorway.
shots.accepted_variant: Reviewed returned-shopping scene also retains Blue at home, identified from actually sent approved 023 seating reference. No claim of sending a separate Blue sheet on this retry.

shots.narration: The city around you is also a seat of government. The shogun's power and the residences of feudal lords help explain why so much demand concentrates here. Goods are not moving into an accidental collection of villages. People with money, rank, and obligations need the city to supply them.
shots.action: Blue crosses the unchanged bridge EMPTY-HANDED, taking in the timber city. No wrapped box here: the customer has not collected it yet. Keep his exact indigo costume and neck towel, no weapons or bags.

shots.narration: The Asian Art Museum points out that artisans and merchants supplied the material wants of the upper classes. It also describes samurai taking on civilian and cultural roles during the long peace. A warrior's status did not mean that every hour of his day involved fighting.
shots.action: Fixed market wide shot with an anonymous adult white-headed official in charcoal long sleeves and trousers inspecting a plain cloth-wrapped purchase; no sword battle, no armor.

shots.narration: Some merchants accumulated wealth that exceeded that of samurai. That helps break a misleading picture: status on one side, money on the other, each perfectly matching. They did not always match. Nor did every person called a merchant possess the resources of a great commercial household.
shots.action: Green stands behind the fixed vegetable counter, calmly arranging one small basket of greens; no gold treasure or rich palace.

shots.narration: A customer reaches the workshop. He is the same shopkeeper your partner will encounter at the produce counter, now looking after a need of his own. You place the box between you and lift the lid. He can inspect what he is taking away before the parcel is wrapped.
shots.action: Blue demonstrates the completed matching box lid fit to Green by lifting it; original box and tools remain; it will be closed for wrapping before Green leaves.
shots.accepted_variant: Reviewed lid-demonstration pose fits customer handover; box not replaced or duplicated.

shots.narration: The parcel leaves. Your attention turns to the next object rather than following it to every place it will go. This is not the end of the day, just the end of one job. From the street, the workshop looks much the same. From inside, there is now room for something else.
shots.action: Green exits the fixed RIGHT workshop doorway carrying that SAME small wide shallow box CLOSED, now wrapped in plain GRAY cloth with ONE knot. Keep its wide shallow silhouette, not a cube or round bundle. Blue out of this shot. Original hand plane/mallet/chisel remain on bench; box no longer on bench because Green is carrying the ONLY one.

shots.narration: Now the coins matter. The Bank of Japan's Currency Museum describes the Edo shogunate's gold, silver, and copper currencies. They did not all work in exactly the same way. Gold carried denominations, silver was weighed, and copper coins served as smaller units of exchange.
shots.action: Red stands at the fixed produce counter opposite Green; a few small plain copper coins lie on the counter, no giant gold coin or modern yen.

shots.narration: Take fewer vegetables, or choose something else. Keep a little back, or spend it now. Such choices are not unique to Edo, which is precisely why they are useful. They make an unfamiliar monetary system feel less like a display case and more like somebody's afternoon.
shots.action: Red selects a small radish from the fixed basket while holding her woven shopping basket with the other white mitten hand, no exaggerated expression.

shots.narration: For the seller, a customer is one part of another working day. The goods must be arranged and moved. A person pausing over a choice can delay the next task without meaning to. Our market is full of these small collisions between somebody's convenience and somebody else's workload.
shots.action: Green lifts one modest woven vegetable basket onto the fixed counter, no shoulder pole or extra props, same identity as reference.

shots.narration: But Edo also offered ways to eat without preparing everything yourself. The Tokyo Metropolitan Library explains how the city's large population of male retainers and employees helped create demand for food services. The meal could come from somebody whose occupation was making it available to other people.
shots.action: Blue pauses beside an anonymous covered adult white-headed ochre vendor at the fixed market; vendor carries a small plain lidded wooden food tray, no sushi.

shots.narration: After the great fire of sixteen fifty-seven, the influx of reconstruction workers helped expand the trade in prepared food. Sellers offered cooked or grilled fish and vegetables. That history gives us a better lunchtime image than projecting every later famous Edo dish backward onto the year seventeen hundred.
shots.action: Close shot of a plain wooden tray on the fixed market counter with a single modest cooked fish and a small dish of vegetables; no nigiri sushi, fried tempura or modern paper wrapper.

shots.narration: For our worker, the pause is simple. A bowl, a place to sit, and a few minutes when the workbench is out of reach. The setting is illustrative, not a named establishment. What matters is the exchange: someone else's preparation gives you a break from your own.
shots.action: Blue sits alone on LEFT portion of the ONE original near/right bench, in the same position as Blue in the last approved seating reference. ONE rice bowl, ONE small vegetable dish and ONE tea cup on table left within his reach. THREE counter cups and rounded kettle remain unchanged. No rear bench, parcel, Red or Green.

shots.narration: The shopkeeper sits beside you with his new parcel. The work you delivered has become an object resting beside a bench. For a moment, neither of you is discussing the fit of a lid or tending a vegetable counter. There are other things worth noticing in the city.
shots.action: Blue remains seated on LEFT portion and Green now sits on RIGHT portion of that SAME original near/right bench. Two tea cups on table, one each. Blue's rice bowl and vegetable dish remain on table left, now mostly emptied after lunch. Green's SAME wide shallow box, wrapped in GRAY cloth with one knot, rests on bench at Green's outer RIGHT side. No cube/bag. THREE counter cups and kettle remain. No additional bench.
shots.accepted_variant: Retry with approved actual meal and wrapped parcel state, not text alone.

shots.narration: It is a pleasant pause. The customer's morning and yours have crossed here, after hours spent on different tasks. Eating together does not give you identical lives. It gives you a stretch of shared time before each of you returns to the business that brought you through the streets.
shots.action: Blue and Green BOTH remain seated in the same seats on the ONE original near/right bench. Both rest their mitten hands calmly on knees. TWO tea cups, mostly emptied rice bowl and vegetable dish remain on table left. Green's GRAY wrapped wide shallow box remains at his outer RIGHT side on bench. Do not erase Green, the meal dishes, the second cup or the parcel.
shots.accepted_variant: State/color retry using specifically reviewed actual props, not textual descriptions alone.

shots.narration: In a little while, somebody stands up first. The conversation can wait; the next job cannot. There is no alarm in our scene. Just a movement that changes two people sharing a table into one person sitting and another person on his way somewhere else.
shots.action: Green stands up beside RIGHT end of original bench and picks up his SAME GRAY cloth-wrapped wide shallow box, one knot. Blue remains seated on LEFT portion. TWO tea cups plus emptied rice bowl/vegetable dish remain on table. No duplicate parcel left on bench. THREE counter cups and kettle remain unchanged. No rear bench.
shots.accepted_variant: State/color retry using specifically reviewed actual props, not textual descriptions alone.

shots.narration: The waterfront makes the city's dependence easier to see. The Tokyo Metropolitan Library describes land and sea distribution bringing produce and seafood into Edo. The large city does not live only on what is growing beside its own streets. It consumes the work of a much larger hinterland.
shots.action: Blue stands beside the fixed bridge railing looking toward the moored wooden cargo boat and straw-wrapped bundles at landing; no modern harbor.

shots.narration: At the landing, a boat lies close to bundles and a warehouse. Before any goods can reach a shop, somebody must shift them from one place to another. Distribution is a large word. The visible work is often a very specific load that needs to be carried.
shots.action: Close framing toward the fixed landing with modest straw-wrapped bundles, wooden boat and timber warehouse doorway; no labels, no new bridge angle.

shots.narration: A person carrying a bundle across the bridge sees the same place differently from somebody admiring the water. For Green, the route is useful. For you, it may briefly be restful. Work and pleasure can occupy the same view without occupying the same person's time.
shots.action: Green crosses original bridge carrying his SAME wide shallow finished wooden box wrapped in GRAY cloth with ONE knot. Copy proportions from final box reference: a modest flat rectangular parcel, not a cube or shopping bag. Same jade jacket, charcoal trousers and gray sash.

shots.narration: You lean near the railing and watch a boat for a moment. The city has not stopped; your participation in it has changed. In the workshop you made something. At the stall you bought something. Here, briefly, you are not completing a transaction at all.
shots.action: Blue rests both white mitten hands lightly on the fixed bridge railing, watching the moored boat; no added ship crew.

shots.narration: Back in the workshop, a fresh board waits. But first you clear the shavings from the workbench. In a city of timber buildings and open flames, the relationship between ordinary activity and fire is never entirely theoretical. Cooking and lighting provide necessities. They also provide sources of danger.
shots.action: Blue gathers a few wood shavings from the fixed workbench into a small plain wooden tray; hand plane lies safely beside a fresh board.

shots.narration: The Tokyo Fire Department describes dense wooden housing and everyday use of flame as conditions that made fire dangerous. The buildings stand close together. A small household problem can therefore become somebody else's problem very quickly. You do not need a fire today to have a reason to remember that.
shots.action: Use the unchanged approved empty location master as the establishing environment for this narration.

shots.narration: The great fire of sixteen fifty-seven had changed the city. The Tokyo Metropolitan Library describes relocation, wider routes, and new development after the catastrophe. Our ordinary day happens after that rebuilding. Disaster is not the action we are staging, but it helps explain the city around the action.
shots.action: Use the unchanged approved empty location master as the establishing environment for this narration.

shots.narration: Your partner brings the cooking pot safely toward the room. Heating and preparing food have taken attention, as well as ingredients. The meal is nearly ready, but it can wait until you return from washing. She sets the pot where it can be kept safely, then gathers a cloth.

You leave the next board and put the tools away. The remaining work needs another stretch of concentration, and there are other things to do before night. Leaving the bench in order makes the next start easier. For today, the workshop has supplied enough tasks.
shots.action: Blue puts the small hand plane and mallet neatly at the back of the fixed bench; window daylight still soft, no written clock.

shots.narration: By later in the day, washing has its own destination. The Tokyo bathhouse association describes public baths becoming popular during the Edo period, linking their growth to restrictions on private baths intended to prevent fires. Water and heating could be concentrated in a business instead of repeated in every house.
shots.action: Blue approaches the fixed modest bathhouse entrance with a folded plain gray cloth held in one white mitten hand; entirely clothed, no bathing.

shots.narration: For our household, a visit is another small purchase and another journey. Carry what you need. Go there rather than expecting hot water to be waiting in your room. The activity is familiar; the arrangement around it differs. Convenience has a location, and you must reach it.
shots.action: Red stands beside the fixed bathhouse outdoor bench holding a folded plain burgundy cloth; fully covered long sleeves and trousers.

shots.narration: You meet outside again after washing, dressed for the trip onward. It feels good to have dealt with the dust and effort of the day. There is still a meal ahead, and perhaps time for a brief detour before going home. Neither of you has to stand at the workbench now.
shots.action: Blue and Red stand outside unchanged bathhouse doorway in the same clothes. Blue holds ONE folded plain GRAY cloth, matching his earlier bath approach, not a blue handbag. Red holds ONE folded plain BURGUNDY cloth. No bags, skin steam, outfit change or undressing.

shots.narration: With the workshop's tools left behind and the purchases already home, you can walk without watching a heavy bundle. The street is the same, but the task attached to it has changed. A little farther on, the theater entrance attracts your attention.
shots.action: Blue and Red walk back along unchanged alley. Blue carries the SAME folded plain GRAY bath cloth; Red carries the SAME folded plain BURGUNDY bath cloth. No basket, tool bundle, handbag, blue bag or weapons.

shots.narration: And somewhere in the city, the question is not what needs finishing but what is worth watching. The Tokyo Metropolitan Library describes kabuki gaining greater public acceptance in Edo by the end of the seventeenth century. Entertainment belongs to this city, not merely to its later reputation.
shots.action: Green stands outside the fixed theater entrance with hands resting by his sides, looking at the burgundy doorway curtain; no ticket in hand.

shots.narration: Going inside would require more time and money than a brief look. You stop outside instead. You can be curious about a performance without making it today's outing. A future visit is a possibility to consider, alongside the other things the household wants.
shots.action: Canonical theater exterior with three distant anonymous adult white-headed townspeople in covered muted clothes near the entrance; no evening lantern relighting.

shots.narration: You can be interested without entering. Stop near the display. Look at the illustrations. Notice somebody else's excitement. A city's entertainment reaches farther than the people who pay for a seat on a particular occasion. It can become a subject of talk before it becomes your own outing.
shots.action: Blue and Red stand at the fixed small display stand looking at two monochrome sheets showing simple architectural stage motifs, not human actor faces, no readable writing.

shots.narration: The Met connects Edo's urban arts with kabuki and the prints called ukiyo-e. Black-and-white woodblock pictures belong to this early world too: its collection includes a print dated seventeen hundred. The elaborate full-color culture familiar from later prints was still to develop.
shots.action: Empty close view of the same display stand. Preserve EXACTLY the two black-and-white pictures visible in reference image 2: roofed timber facade on LEFT, timber stage interior on RIGHT. Do not substitute a bridge, river or another scene. No people anywhere.

shots.narration: The shopkeeper recognizes you beside the display. His parcel has gone elsewhere. You have both completed things since the lunchtime pause, and there are new things to mention. A few minutes of talk let the neighborhood expand beyond the places you personally visited.
shots.action: Blue and Green converse beside the same display stand. shots.narration: Books and prints also carried information and entertainment into the city. The Edo-Tokyo Museum describes publishing as a growing part of its culture. A picture on a display and a book in a shop belong to an urban world interested in more than supplies and official orders.

shots.narration: For our couple, today's leisure is a seat by the water, not a major spectacle. Two cups arrive. There is enough time to sit rather than carrying everything onward. You are still in the working city. The difference is that, for a moment, somebody else is tending the counter.

shots.narration: The shopkeeper passes and stops to exchange a few words before going on. He has been a buyer, a seller, and a companion at different points in the day. Those roles belong to one person, not separate types of people permanently assigned to separate backgrounds.
shots.action: Blue LEFT and Red RIGHT still sit on ONE original near/right bench, with TWO cups on table and the SAME woven basket with greens/food parcel on ground beside RIGHT bench end. Green stands one pace to RIGHT of bench, EMPTY-HANDED, stopping briefly. THREE counter cups and kettle retained; no extra bench or parcel.

shots.narration: Eventually, the cups are empty. You leave the bench to somebody else. The pause has not solved the household's next expense or shortened tomorrow's work. It has done something less spectacular: given the day a stretch that was not entirely organized around completing a task.
shots.action: Blue and Red now stand beside the ONE original near/right bench. Red lifts the SAME woven basket with greens/food parcel from ground beside RIGHT bench end. TWO EMPTY cups remain on table in their original positions. THREE counter cups and kettle unchanged. No third table cup, no duplicate basket, no new bench.

shots.narration: At home, the evening meal is ready to reach the table. Your partner brings the bowls while you clear a place. The water fetched this morning and the food carried from the market have led here. You sit opposite one another in a room familiar enough to find things without searching.

Two rice bowls, two soup bowls and ONE vegetable dish. SAME woven basket now inside RIGHT doorway on floor, no other cushion or new furniture.

Blue gathers the EXACT gray rolled tool wrap with single tie and wooden handle ends at table LEFT. SAME woven shopping basket remains on floor inside RIGHT doorway. ONE cushion remains LEFT; Red on bare tatami.

shots.narration: You check the tool bundle before putting it aside. The next job has not been done in advance. Tomorrow will still ask for work. But knowing where the tools are is one problem you do not need to solve again at the start of it.

shots.narration: What did people in Edo actually do all day? Our artisan household has made things, exchanged them, bought food, carried supplies, eaten, washed, and found a little time to enjoy the city. Somebody else's day would contain different work and a different balance, but it would be just as full of practical details.
shots.action: Empty fixed workshop bench with plain board, hand plane and small mallet neatly arranged for next day; daylight reference as reflective recap not night continuity.

shots.narration: The urban world joined people through those details. Craftsmen and merchants supplied its needs and shaped parts of its culture. They also faced unequal resources and status. A seller's chance to earn was another household's chance to eat, and your finished work became a useful object in somebody else's home.
shots.action: Green tends the fixed produce counter, jade long-sleeved jacket and charcoal trousers unchanged, one basket of radishes and one of greens.

shots.narration: The seat by the water was part of the answer too. Free time was uneven, and a pleasant pause did not erase an obligation. Still, it mattered. If you only saw the couple relaxing, you would miss the work; if you only saw the work, you would miss what made the day worth finishing.
shots.action: Reflective recap deliberately reuses the reviewed later tea scene 080, keeping both characters, both cups and Red's basket unchanged.
shots.accepted_variant: Intentional exact-image recap of shot 080, not a separately generated state.

shots.narration: Tonight the room is ready to be a sleeping place again. The box is finished. The basket is home. The bowls are cleared. Tomorrow will rearrange much of it once more. For now, the last task is to let the day end, in one small household in Edo.
